newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Refugees stream back to Rwanda from Tanzania.
newsitem.headline: Refugees stream back to Rwanda from Tanzania.

text.p: Thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees flooded back into their homeland from Tanzania on Sunday and officials at the remote Rusomo border post west of Lake Victoria said about 9,000 crossed over during the night.
The post, normally closed at night, remained open to allow the flow of refugees, the second major mass repatriation into Rwanda in five weeks, to continue.

At dawn on Sunday thousands who had bedded down in the open overnight, some cooking frugal meals over wood fires, resumed their trek towards Rusomo. They crossed in a steady stream, estimated by witnesses at a thousand an hour.
Aid workers said most of the refugees arriving at the border had come from camps south of the large Benaco camp at Ngara.
They had been shepherded past the Benaco camp by Tanzanian security forces to keep them moving towards the border.
"Many people are walking in the right direction," said Anne Willem Bijleveld of the United Nations refugee agency UNHCR.

He said 2,000 to 3,000 had crossed into Rwanda by the Rusomo crossing by nightfall on Saturday and an estimated 50,000 more were in a column on the 17-km (11-mile) road from Benaco camp, the largest in Tanzania, to the border.
The exodus followed talks between camp leaders in Benaco and officials of the Tanzanian government, which says it wants all 540,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees in Tanzania out by December 31.

"It looks now as if the army has things under control," said Bijleveld, adding that it had dropped earlier restrictions to limit the UNHCR's assistance in the government's mass repatriation operation.
He said soldiers walked with refugees but "in a humane manner" and even assisted the needy.
Shortly after dark, the Red Cross estimated that 500 were still crossing the border every hour.
Before the column reached the border on Saturday, witnesses said hundreds of thousands were streaming towards Rusomo from as far away as Nyakahura, about 100 km (60 miles) to the southeast.
Aid agencies set up water points, health posts and biscuit distribution sites along a 100-km route from the Rwanda border.
About 200,000 of the refugees originally came from villages within 30 km (18 miles) of the Rusomo crossing and were expected to walk back to their former homes.

U.N. aid officials said they believed a rush away from the border by hundreds of thousands of refugees on Thursday broke the grip of the Hutu intimidators who had ordered the refugees not to try to return to Rwanda.
Troops and police turned back most of the refugees who had earlier headed inland into Tanzania from their camps, encouraging them instead to walk towards the Rwanda border.

It was unclear whether any action was being taken by Tanzanian security forces to restrain the Hutu militiamen and former Rwandan troops, who fear to return because of involvement in the genocide of up to a million people in Rwanda in 1994.
In addition to more than 500,000 Rwandan refugees, there were 112,000 Burundian refugees in Tanzania.
The latest migration was the second mass return of Rwandan refugees. More than 500,000 left Zaire in four days from November 15 after a rebellion by Zairean Tutsis broke the Hutu intimidators' hold.
The U.N. has ordered 350 Canadian servicemen and women, the basis of a multinational force destined for eastern Zaire, to pull out and return home from their bases in Uganda and Rwanda.

The force, formed in mid-November, was rejected by the Zairean rebels who control a large slice of eastern Zaire. It was unable to help Rwandan refugees in Zaire and failed to win the support of other nations who might have contributed troops.
Canadian spokesmen said the troops would start leaving on Monday and the last would be home by the end of the month.
African leaders including South Africa's President Nelson Mandela are to meet in Nairobi on Monday to discuss efforts to control the conflict in Zaire and the Great Lakes region of Central Africa.
